safety_layer2.search_summary:
Here is a comprehensive summary of all major safety-related regulatory actions involving **Brexanolone (brand name: Zulresso®)**:

---

## ✅ Yes — Brexanolone Has Been Withdrawn, Had a Black Box Warning, and Been Discontinued

---

### 1. 🚫 Market Withdrawal & FDA Approval Revocation (2024–2025)


Sage Therapeutics took Zulresso off the market on December 31, 2024, citing the need to focus on zuranolone.
 
The manufacturer withdrew brexanolone to focus on its oral version – zuranolone (Zurzuvae).


Following this, 
the FDA withdrew approval of the New Drug Application (NDA) for ZULRESSO (brexanolone) solution, 100 mg/20 mL, held by Sage Therapeutics, Inc., after Sage notified the Agency in writing that the drug product was no longer marketed and requested that the approval be withdrawn. Approval was withdrawn as of **April 14, 2025**.



This drug has been discontinued in the United States.


📎 **Source (Federal Register – Official FDA Notice):** https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/03/14/2025-04101/sage-therapeutics-inc-withdrawal-of-approval-of-a-new-drug-application-for-zulresso-brexanolone

---

### 2. ⚠️ Black Box (Boxed) Warning

Brexanolone carried the FDA's most serious drug warning — a **Boxed (Black Box) Warning** — from the time of its approval.


**Box Warnings: Excessive sedation and loss of consciousness** — Patients are at risk of experiencing extreme sedation or sudden loss of consciousness during brexanolone administration.



There was an FDA Black Box Warning for Zulresso for excessive sedation and sudden loss of consciousness. As a result, healthcare facilities were required to enroll in the FDA's REMS (Risk Evaluation and Management Strategy) for Zulresso.



The major safety concern observed with brexanolone was that six subjects experienced loss of consciousness/syncope/presyncope during infusion. Of these six, one fainted with blood draw, one suffered presyncope/vertigo while standing, and four appeared to have suddenly fallen asleep. These effects were resolved with dose interruption and all patients recovered in 10 to 60 minutes. The FDA noted that the loss of consciousness can be abrupt, and there is no known way to predict the risk, which could result in serious harm, accident, or injury to the mother and, potentially, to the infant.



Brexanolone had black box warnings for severe sedation and loss of consciousness, which occurred in 5% of patients, managed by stopping the infusion with symptoms resolving in 90 minutes or less.


📎 **Source (StatPearls/NCBI):** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541054/
📎 **Source (Drugs.com Monograph):** https://www.drugs.com/monograph/brexanolone.html
📎 **Source (Drugs.com – Patient Safety):** https://www.drugs.com/cons/brexanolone.html

---

### 3. 🔒 Restricted Distribution via REMS Program

Because of the Black Box Warning risks, the drug was never freely dispensed. 
Because of these risks, brexanolone was available only through a restricted program under a **Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)** called the Zulresso REMS.



Brexanolone carried a Boxed Warning and had to be prescribed through a special REMS program. This meant it was only available at healthcare facilities that had been specifically certified through the brexanolone REMS program, and the patient's information had to be registered before treatment was given.


📎 **Source (Simple and Practical Mental Health):** https://simpleandpractical.com/brexanolone-zulresso/

---

### 4. 📋 Was It Withdrawn for Safety Reasons?

Importantly, the withdrawal was **not due to a new safety crisis or post-market safety signal**. 
The manufacturer withdrew brexanolone to focus on its oral version – zuranolone (Zurzuvae).
 It was a **voluntary, commercial/strategic decision** by Sage Therapeutics, not a regulatory safety-forced withdrawal. However, the drug did carry significant safety concerns (Black Box Warning, REMS) throughout its entire time on the market.


Any brexanolone solution in inventory as of April 14, 2025, may continue to be dispensed until the inventory has been depleted or the drug products have reached their expiration dates.


📎 **Source (Carlat Psychiatry Report):** https://www.thecarlatreport.com/blogs/2-the-carlat-psychiatry-podcast/post/5445-so-long-brexanolone

---

### Summary Table

| Event | Details |
|---|---|
| **FDA Approval** | March 2019 |
| **Black Box Warning** | Yes – from initial approval; excessive sedation & sudden loss of consciousness |
| **REMS Program** | Yes – restricted to certified healthcare facilities |
| **Market Discontinuation** | December 31, 2024 (by manufacturer, Sage Therapeutics) |
| **FDA Approval Withdrawn** | April 14, 2025 |
| **Reason for Withdrawal** | Commercial/strategic (shift to oral zuranolone), not a new safety-driven recall |

mechanism_direction.disease_mechanism_summary:
Here is the target-focused assessment for **PRASTERONE (DHEA)** in **Class I glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency**.

## 1) Disease mechanism

**Core defect:** **Class I G6PD deficiency is a loss-of-function disorder of G6PD**, not an overactivity state. Class I variants are the most severe category and are associated with **chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia (CNSHA)**, typically with **<10% residual G6PD activity** in erythrocytes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10281211/?utm_source=openai))

At the molecular level, the primary mechanism is **pathogenic G6PD mutation causing unstable and/or catalytically impaired enzyme**, which reduces NADPH generation through the pentose phosphate pathway. In red cells, that means impaired maintenance of reduced glutathione and defective protection from oxidative stress, leading to ongoing hemolysis; severe Class I variants are especially linked to **protein instability and impaired enzyme function**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3382019/?utm_source=openai))

**Answer to Q1:** **G6PD is DEFICIENT (reduced/lost function)** in Class I G6PD deficiency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10281211/?utm_source=openai))

## 2) Target-specific direction for prasterone on G6PD

For the **direct action on G6PD itself**, the literature identifies **dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA; prasterone)** as an **inhibitor of mammalian/human G6PD**, including descriptions as a **non-competitive** or **uncompetitive** inhibitor depending on assay/system. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/71/4_Supplement/S114/6841648?utm_source=openai))

Because the disease defect in Class I G6PD deficiency is already **too little G6PD activity**, a drug that directly **inhibits G6PD** would be expected to **worsen**, not correct or compensate for, the primary defect. This conclusion is strictly about the **drug’s direct effect on G6PD**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10281211/?utm_source=openai))

**Answer to Q2:** Based on known direct pharmacology, **prasterone would be expected to WORSEN the disease defect at the G6PD target level**, because it inhibits an enzyme that is already deficient. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/71/4_Supplement/S114/6841648?utm_source=openai))

## 3) Clinical use anchor

I found **no evidence that prasterone/DHEA is an approved or established investigational treatment for Class I G6PD deficiency** or for a disease caused by **G6PD dysfunction via a therapeutic mechanism of restoring G6PD**. Current references on G6PD deficiency management emphasize avoidance of oxidative triggers and supportive care, and reviews note the lack of specific disease-modifying therapy in routine practice. ([merckmanuals.com](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology-and-oncology/anemias-caused-by-hemolysis/glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase-g6pd-deficiency?ruleredirectid=382&utm_source=openai))

By contrast, **prasterone is approved as INTRAROSA for dyspareunia due to vulvar/vaginal atrophy of menopause**, not for G6PD-related disease, and its approved labeling does not describe a therapeutic mechanism through G6PD. ([dailymed.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=ada639d4-bac0-2ad0-e053-2a95a90afce7&utm_source=openai))

There is experimental literature showing DHEA can **inhibit G6PD** in biochemical/cell systems, but that is the opposite of the direction needed for Class I deficiency and does **not** constitute a validated treatment mechanism for G6PD-deficient disease. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC287239/?page=4&utm_source=openai))

**Answer to Q3:** **No** — prasterone (and the closely related compound DHEA) is **not known as an approved or clinically validated treatment for Class I G6PD deficiency through G6PD**. Its confirmed approved use is unrelated to G6PD deficiency, and the best-supported direct G6PD mechanism in the literature is **enzyme inhibition**, not restoration/activation. ([dailymed.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=ada639d4-bac0-2ad0-e053-2a95a90afce7&utm_source=openai))

## Bottom line

- **Disease biology:** Class I G6PD deficiency = **G6PD loss/reduction of function**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10281211/?utm_source=openai))
- **Drug-on-target direction:** Prasterone/DHEA is reported to **inhibit G6PD**, so direct action on G6PD would **worsen** the primary defect. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/ejendo/article/71/4_Supplement/S114/6841648?utm_source=openai))
- **Clinical anchor:** No approved or validated G6PD-restorative use of prasterone for this disease was found. ([dailymed.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=ada639d4-bac0-2ad0-e053-2a95a90afce7&utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can also turn this into a compact **repurposing verdict table** with columns like *disease direction*, *drug direction*, *match/mismatch*, and *confidence*.
